paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A p-value answers one question: if the null hypothesis were correct, how probable would it be to get test results at least as extreme as the ones actually seen? The null hypothesis is the default claim that some property does not exist, typically that a parameter such as a difference between means is zero. A very small p-value means an outcome this extreme would be very unlikely if the null hypothesis held.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The p-value is how null hypothesis testing puts a number on the statistical significance of a result. A result counts as statistically significant if it lets us reject the null hypothesis. All else being equal, a smaller p-value is taken as stronger evidence against that hypothesis. Reporting p-values is common practice in academic papers across many quantitative fields, yet misreading and misusing them is widespread and has become a major topic in mathematics and metascience.

paragraphs.heading: Working it out
paragraphs.text: The data are usually reduced to a single number, a statistic T, tied closely to the main question of the study. A one-sided right-tail test uses p = Pr (T ≥ t ∣ H₀), and a one-sided left-tail test uses p = Pr (T ≤ t ∣ H₀). When the distribution of T is symmetric about zero, p = Pr (|T| ≥ |t| ∣ H₀).

paragraphs.heading: Drawing the line
paragraphs.text: The null hypothesis is rejected when the p-value falls below a threshold α, called the alpha level or significance level. The researcher sets α before looking at the data rather than deriving it from them. It is commonly 0.05, though lower levels are sometimes used. That 0.05 value, a 1 in 20 chance, was first proposed by Ronald Fisher in 1925 in his book Statistical Methods for Research Workers.

paragraphs.heading: What it cannot tell you
paragraphs.text: Rejecting a null hypothesis can mean several different things. If the null says a statistic T has the standard normal distribution N (0, 1), a rejection could mean the mean of T is not 0, the variance is not 1, or T is not normal at all. Even when we know the distribution is normal with variance 1, the test does not say which non-zero means are now most plausible. More independent observations make the test more accurate, but they also make it more important to ask whether the deviation matters in the real world.

paragraphs.heading: A number that moves
paragraphs.text: Because the p-value is a function of the test statistic, it is itself a random variable. If the null hypothesis fixes the distribution of T precisely and that distribution is continuous, the p-value is spread evenly between 0 and 1 whenever the null is true. Repeat the same test on fresh data and you will typically get a different p-value each time. When many studies on one subject are gathered, the distribution of their significant p-values, called a p-curve, can reveal publication bias or p-hacking.
